"Shock, shock! I learned yesterday that an open problem I’d been working on for several weeks had just
been solved by Claude Opus 4.6."

https://cs.stanford.edu/~knuth/papers/claude-cycles.pdf
The end times for new entrants into math research is really here now isn’t it , who will even need a post-doc !

Hmm, I wonder how much Lean is on Don’s radar, in particular when it comes to “AI writes a proof, let’s be double sure of it”. He does not mention it in the text.

Is someone already feeding that paper to aristotle (or just claude) for a Lean formalization? If there is lots of Buzz about „Don talks about Claude“ it may be good if some of that buzz is „and of course there is a Lean proof of this now“.

Joachim Breitner said:

Is someone already feeding that paper to aristotle (or just claude) for a Lean formalization?

Yes, see https://x.com/tummycom/status/2029017752984514934 and their repo https://github.com/evelynmitchell/ClaudesCyclesLean
Though at first glance this looks terrible, they aren't using any of mathlib's graph theory

Snir Broshi said:

Joachim Breitner said:

Is someone already feeding that paper to aristotle (or just claude) for a Lean formalization?

Yes, see https://x.com/tummycom/status/2029017752984514934 and their repo https://github.com/evelynmitchell/ClaudesCyclesLean
Though at first glance this looks terrible, they aren't using any of mathlib's graph theory

In their defense mathlib's graph theory APIs leave much to be desired (squints at lack of vertex sets in Simplegraphs)
I have found myself inventing definitions for such basic things as cycles in directed graphs.
It is impossible to blame anybody for not using mathlib graphs.
No I think in this case it is possible. It's not like they defined their own version of a graph, they did whatever this is
I haven’t read the paper but it looks like they are dealing with some sort of a 3 regular graph or a graph with cycles.
And it’s actually much simpler to work with it this way than try to integrate it with even the SimpleGraph api, and here they are working with Digraphs, whose API is close to non-existent.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

I haven’t read the paper but it looks like they are dealing with some sort of a 3 regular graph or a graph with cycles.

It's a 3d cube with edges going in the positive x,y,z directions, so 3-regular but in the directed sense

I think it's easier and more sensible to complete the digraph API (in their own repo) rather than to conjure up some strange way to represent a graph that isn't faithful to the paper. But I haven't tried yet, so idk
Well, for one thing nobody has adopted to complete my digraph PR
Even though i put that label last week
So clearly that process is slow.

And repeat that across the whole digraph API + mathlib review time cycles and one wonders whether digraph’s API will even achieve parity with SimpleGraph by end of year. And this shouldn’t go the AI way in any case.

Instead we have a simple representation of 3 regular graphs and cycles that seems simple enough and “just works”. Also the formalization seems relatively clean and easy to check unlike the AI slop we regularly see on Zulip these days

I don’t think everyone adopting formalization will and should wait for mathlib’s slow process to formalise their work. They should make sensible (non-AI-slop) formalisations and the community should encourage them to upstream what they can.

But at the end of the day it is upto mathlib’s community to come up with a way to scale the contributions process to accommodate 10 to 20 times the PRs it manages today with a much more timely review cycle. I am sure we are all individually doing our best, especially reviewers and maintainers, but this is a scaling problem and there needs to be a substantially larger organisation of reviewers and maintainers, which also requires resources.

To be clear this is not a suggestion to invite more AI slop. Slop remains slop by rfl.

Joachim Breitner said:

Hmm, I wonder how much Lean is on Don’s radar, in particular when it comes to “AI writes a proof, let’s be double sure of it”. He does not mention it in the text.

As far as I can see, he isn't claiming that AI wrote the proof, but rather that AI found a suitably general example that he then proved (and that finding such a general example, not proving it, was the hard part of the problem in this case).

Shreyas Srinivas said:

So clearly that process is slow.

Yeah the Mathlib contribution process is slow, but I'm not talking about that. There shouldn't be anything slow about completing the digraph API in their own repo
I make no claims re quality but Claude, Aristotle, and I took a go at formalising this here: https://github.com/septract/claudes-cycles-lean
I’d welcome feedback (not least because I’m curious whether Claude could successfully implement the feedback)
@Mike Dodds well done, you beat me to it. For comparison, here is a pure Claude (and very little me!) formalization: https://github.com/kim-em/KnuthClaudeLean
And it now uses @Henrik Böving's comparator, since I am a good citizen and treat AI generated proofs with suspicion :wink:.
I would love to get news of this back to Knuth...

@Kim Morrison nice! In my development Claude managed to prove Cycle1 while Aristotle was working, so that proof is more cleanly structured. I like Aristotle but the proofs it produces are quite messy.

Also: I didn’t know about ‘comparator’, that looks v useful. Along similar lines, I recently built a little tool called lean-tcb which tries to identify the theorems / definitions etc you should audit in order to trust a proof https://github.com/OathTech/lean-tcb

here is a pure Claude (and very little me!) formalization: https://github.com/kim-em/KnuthClaudeLean

Nice! It's the first solution that uses actual graphs

You'd have to ask Claude --- I had zero input into the maths. I told it:

  • download this PDF
  • split into pages
  • convert into markdown
  • have codex check your translation
  • analyze the theorem statements, and decide what the results on the path to the "main result" are
  • research what is available in Mathlib that is relevant to formalizing this material
  • write Lean statements proved by sorry
  • have codex check these statements faithfully reflect the material
  • write a PLAN.md for filling in all the sorries
  • prove all the sorries (this one took a few sessions, but with no real prompting beyond "keep working on the sorries")

Throwing in one more vibe/slop proof - https://github.com/rkirov/claude-cycles-lean (see README for the full story). I only used claude code.
One thing that bothers me about this proof is how long a fresh lake build takes for a proof doesn't seem that long. Tempted to run an unscientific local benchmark between the 3 vibeproofs.
also anyone grinding the even case which doesn't have a knuth proof either? I was thinking about starting it tonight.

I had the agent grinding a proof for the even case over the weekend, but it kept getting stuck on lean taking too long to typecheck.

Refetched the original paper and @Kim Morrison and @Kevin Buzzard are now mentioned - https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/papers/claude-cycles.pdf!

Also, it seems chatgpt produced a paper for the even case, but informal. I was hoping to feed that into the claude formalization loop to get some ideas that might produce more efficient proofs, but seems that the link is 404ing.
Most importantly, see the very last part of the note as it now stands.
